# Notes on Isaiah 64 (verse by verse)

**About these notes:** I couldn't find anything on these sites from Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), Orthodox sources (oca.org), bibleodyssey.org, or prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teachers. The only Lutheran material is a Luther saying quoted by the Puritan John Trapp, at v. 6. The real Protestant split is over v. 6, with v. 5 linked to it.

---

**v. 1**
- **Context:** Guzik reads this as the remnant's prayer from Isaiah 63 going on. It asks God to step in from heaven.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-64/
- **Like Sinai:** The Pulpit Commentary says Israel is asking God to show himself, as he did when he "came down" on Mount Sinai. Mountains stand for the firmest things on earth. If even they shake before him, his power is beyond measure. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/64.htm
- **"Rend":** Barnes says the word means to tear apart, like tearing clothes in grief. It is language properly expressive of a purpose to execute wrath on his foes, rather than to confer blessings on his people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-64.html
- **Wesley (Methodist):** "Rend" pictures someone breaking open doors to rescue a person in trouble. possibly an allusion to God's coming down upon mount Sinai https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-64.html
- **NET notes (scholarly):** The Hebrew Bible places the chapter break differently, so this verse is 63:19b there. The verb is better read as "quake," which may echo Judges 5:5, the only other place it is used. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=64
- **Pointing to Christ:** The Sermon Bible Commentary says God, appearing in Christ, does indeed rend the heavens and come down. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/sbc/isaiah-64.html

**v. 2**
- **Fire and brushwood:** The Pulpit Commentary prefers "as when fire kindles brushwood." Mountains can no more resist God than brushwood or water can resist fire. Such an appearance would make his Name known to the nations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/64.htm
- **Melt or shake?** Barnes notes that the Hebrew word means brushwood. He thinks the main picture is fierce heat melting the mountains, although the lexicon writer Gesenius took the verb as "shake." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-64.html
- **Wesley:** God's enemies would come to know his power, and his name would be feared among them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-64.html

**v. 3**
- **The Exodus:** The Pulpit Commentary says "terrible things" is a standard phrase for the Exodus wonders. "Which we looked not for" means they went beyond all expectation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/64.htm
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** "Camest down" refers to Sinai. far exceeding the expectation of any of our nation https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-64.html
- **Wesley:** The "mountains" may also stand for kings and rulers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-64.html

**v. 4**
- **The only working God:** The Pulpit Commentary prefers the reading "a God beside thee which worketh for him that waiteth upon him." Only the LORD actually acts for his worshippers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/64.htm
- **Paul's use (1 Corinthians 2:9):** Barnes says Paul quotes this verse loosely. He thinks the KJV wording "what he hath prepared" was chosen to match Paul. The Hebrew points instead to what God had already done in the past. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-64.html
- **Ellicott:** St. Paul, in 1 Corinthians 2:9, applies the words freely, after his manner, to the eternal blessings which God prepares for His people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-64.html
- **Wesley:** The verse can apply both to grace now and glory later, the mysteries shown in Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-64.html
- **Waiting:** Guzik says the person praying trusts that because he waits for the LORD, he too will see God act. He quotes Bultema, who says people would rather work than wait. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-64/

**v. 5** (a hard verse, and it shapes how v. 6 is read)
- **The text problem:** The NET notes say the Hebrew literally ends "and we were delivered," which makes little sense here. Some propose a change to "we were evil." NET follows the Hebrew but reads it as a question, "How then can we be saved?" https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=64
- **Many readings:** The Pulpit Commentary lists them. "In those" may mean God's ways or the people's sins, and the last line may be a statement or a question. Delitzsch reads: we have long been in sin, so shall we be saved? https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/64.htm
- **Ellicott** prefers "in the ways of evil we have been a long time, and shall we be saved?" https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-64.html
- **Barnes** also reads it as a question that confesses deep guilt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-64.html
- **Matthew Henry:** "Continuance" means God's lasting mercy and covenant. our hopes of salvation are built not upon any merit or sufficiency of our own https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_064.cfm
- **Benson (Methodist):** Takes a similar line. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/isaiah-64.html
- **Wesley:** Reads it differently: "continuance" is for those that work righteousness, and "be saved" means In so doing, in working righteousness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-64.html
- **The paradox:** Guzik says God answers the prayers of the righteous, yet the ones who need saving are sinners. Only the New Covenant solves this. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-64/

**v. 6** (the main point of disagreement)
- **The traditional reading:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary sees a "moral leprosy." The phrase means "a menstruous garment," and the best deeds of the best people carry some taint. It quotes Hooker, the Anglican: "Our very repentances require to be repented of." https://biblehub.com/isaiah/64-6.htm
  - Ellicott links "unclean" to the leper of Leviticus 13:45 and "filthy rags" to the other most extreme kind of ritual uncleanness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/64-6.htm
  - Barnes says all their prayers, sacrifices and alms were mixed with pollution. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-64.html
  - Guzik, quoting Motyer, says even good works pick up the defilement of fallen human nature. Spurgeon and Clarke thought the Hebrew image too graphic to explain in public. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-64/
- **NET note:** The Hebrew reads "like a garment of menstruation." NET translates "so-called righteous acts." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=64
- **Protestant differences:**
  - *Gill (Baptist, Calvinist):* The verse is about the church's own righteousness, even at its best. It is not about Christ's righteousness credited to believers, which is a spotless robe. It is the language not of a natural man, or of a Pharisee, but of a sensible sinner, a truly gracious soul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/64-6.htm
  - *Piper (Baptist, desiringgod.org):* Calls the "all Christian good works" reading a profoundly mistaken reading of that verse. He points to v. 5, where God welcomes those who joyfully do right. Verse 6, he says, means hypocritical works. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/your-holy-deeds-are-not-filthy-rags
  - *Desiring God article:* Says the same. Good works are evidence of being made right with God, not the ground of it. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/dirty-rags-no-more
  - *Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:* Limits it to the best doings of the unregenerate https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/64-6.htm
  - *Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary:* Our deeds are rags if we think they earn merit with God. Even real works of the Spirit, done by us, are imperfect and need washing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/64-6.htm
  - *Wesley (Methodist):* Reads it as a general falling away from God at that time: Formerly there were some that feared thee. Now even the best are no better than the most unclean. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-64.html
  - *Luther, via Trapp (Puritan):* People who try to be saved by works are what Luther called "the devil's martyrs." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-64/
  - *GotQuestions (evangelical):* The verse first describes Isaiah's own hypocritical Israel. It can still rightly apply to the whole world as an example of total depravity. https://www.gotquestions.org/filthy-rags.html
  - *Biblical Illustrator:* One writer warns against calling filthy rags anything you are in fact right about. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/isaiah-64.html
- **Catholic view (catholic.com):** This pertains to a particular historical situation, not to a general condition. Good works flow from being made right with God (justification). They do not cause it, but they increase the righteousness given and please God. https://www.catholic.com/qa/does-isaiah-646-state-that-good-works-are-useless

**v. 7**
- **A hyperbole:** The Pulpit Commentary says "none calls" is an overstatement; a praying remnant still remained. "Take hold" means intense, fervent prayer. The last line is better "delivered us into the hand of our iniquities": God sometimes hands sinners over to their sins, as in Romans 1. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/64.htm
- **NET:** Follows a change to the Hebrew, "handed us over," meaning God had left them to their sinful ways. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=64
- **Barnes:** "Stir himself up" pictures rousing a person from deep sleep, so the nation was spiritually numb. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-64.html
- **Wesley:** "Take hold" means to stop God leaving, or to bring him back once he has gone. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-64.html
- **Matthew Henry:** "Consumed" can mean "melted," like gold being refined, not thrown away. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_064.cfm
- **Biblical Illustrator:** Taking hold of God means saving faith and wrestling prayer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/isaiah-64.html

**v. 8**
- **Guzik:** The appeal rests on God as Father and as potter. A potter cannot disown the pot he made. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-64/
- **Wesley:** God is Father both by creation, and by adoption https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-64.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Surely God will not abandon the work of his hands (Psalm 138:8). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/64.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** They come back like the prodigal son, under a Father's anger that will not last forever. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_064.cfm

**v. 9**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** God's anger was fierce at the exile (Lamentations 5:22). The exiles hold on to his promise in Isaiah 43:25 that their sin will be not just forgiven but forgotten. "All" means the people taken together. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/64.htm
- **Guzik:** They plead "time served." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-64/
- **Wesley:** Thou hast no people in covenant but us https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-64.html
- **NET:** Another way to translate it: "Take a good look! We are all your people." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=64

**v. 10**
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** "Holy cities" is plural. It may mean the upper and lower parts of Jerusalem (Vitringa) or all the cities of Judea (Maurer). The commentary favours the first. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-64.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Takes it as Judah's cities generally, all within the "holy land." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/64.htm

**v. 11**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The exiles remember the temple's glory (Ezra 3:12) and its burning (2 Kings 25:9). "Pleasant things" probably means the temple courts and grounds. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/64.htm
- **Wesley:** "Pleasant things" means the king's palace and the nobles' houses. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-64.html
- **Barnes:** Treats the prayer as spoken by exiles in Babylon near the end of the captivity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/isaiah-64.html
- **Dating:** A Bible Hub article dates the lament either just before the exile or soon after it. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_righteous_acts_as_filthy_rags.htm
- **Catholic view:** Ties this to the time leading up to Jerusalem's fall in 586 B.C. https://www.catholic.com/qa/does-isaiah-646-state-that-good-works-are-useless

**v. 12**
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Restrain thyself" is better "at these things": will these sights not move God to act? https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/64.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** God's people may trust that their troubles will reach neither to extremity nor to eternity https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_064.cfm
- **Wesley:** Wilt thou be as one that regards not? https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/isaiah-64.html
- **Guzik:** The answer to this prayer comes in the New Covenant: a righteous Man stands in our place and prays for us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-64/
